title: HTML
description: Learn to build the skeleton of every web page with modern HTML5 — from your first tags and headings to forms, tables, and accessible, semantic markup, with hints, explanations, and worked solutions.

roadmap.title: First pages
roadmap.blurb: Build your very first web page. Learn the tags that hold everything together and the words that show on screen.

roadmap.title: Links, pictures & lists
roadmap.blurb: Connect pages with links, add images, and stack your content into neat lists.

roadmap.title: Tables, forms & meaning
roadmap.blurb: Show data in tables, collect answers with forms, and label your page so everyone — including screen readers — understands it.

topics.title: HTML Basics & Structure
topics.description: Learn what HTML is and how a page is built: the doctype, the html, head and body elements, tags, attributes, comments, and metadata.

questions.question: What does HTML stand for?
questions.hint: It is the language for marking up the structure of web pages.
questions.explanation: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language, the standard markup language for documents displayed in a web browser.

questions.question: Which declaration tells the browser the document is written in HTML5?
questions.hint: It is the very first line of a modern page and is short.
questions.explanation: The HTML5 doctype is simply <!DOCTYPE html>; it must be the first thing in the document so the browser uses standards mode.

questions.question: Which element contains the visible content of a page?
questions.hint: It is the sibling of <head> and the part the user actually sees.
questions.explanation: The <body> element holds all the visible content such as text, images, and links, while <head> holds metadata.

questions.question: What do we call the named values inside a tag, like href in <a href="...">, that give extra information about an element?
questions.hint: They live in the opening tag and usually come in name="value" pairs.
questions.explanation: Attributes provide additional information about elements and are written as name="value" pairs inside the opening tag.

questions.question: Which element wraps the entire document and is the root of the HTML tree? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Everything except the doctype lives inside this one element.
questions.explanation: The <html> element is the root element; everything else (head and body) is nested inside it.

questions.question: What is the standard syntax to begin an HTML comment? Give the opening sequence.
questions.hint: It starts with an angle bracket, exclamation mark and two dashes.
questions.explanation: HTML comments are written as <!-- comment -->; the browser ignores anything between the markers.

questions.question: Which meta tag makes a page scale correctly on mobile devices?
questions.hint: It controls the viewport width and initial zoom.
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag with width=device-width, initial-scale=1 tells the browser to match the screen width and not zoom out, which is essential for responsive design.

questions.question: Where does the text shown on the browser tab come from?
questions.hint: It is an element placed inside the <head>.
options: <header> at the top of the body
questions.explanation: The <title> element, placed inside <head>, defines the document title shown in the browser tab and used by search engines and bookmarks.

questions.question: Which meta attribute should be set to "utf-8" so the page can display characters from any language? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It declares the document's character encoding.
questions.explanation: <meta charset="utf-8"> sets the character encoding to UTF-8, which can represent virtually every character and is the recommended default.

questions.question: Write the smallest complete, valid HTML5 page that has the title "My Page" and shows the heading "Hello" in the body.
questions.hint: Start with the doctype, then html, head (with charset and title) and body.
questions.explanation: A minimal HTML5 document needs the doctype, a root <html> element, a <head> with a title (and ideally charset), and a <body> with the visible content.

questions.question: Write the contents of a <head> that sets UTF-8 encoding, a responsive viewport, the page title "Shop", and a meta description of "Best deals online".
questions.hint: You need four elements: charset meta, viewport meta, title, and description meta.
questions.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Shop</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Best deals online">
</head>
questions.explanation: A well-formed head includes encoding, the responsive viewport meta, a descriptive title, and a description meta used by search engines for snippets.

questions.question: Write an HTML comment that says "Navigation starts here" and is invisible to users.
questions.hint: Comments are wrapped in <!-- and -->.
questions.explanation: Text between <!-- and --> is a comment; the browser ignores it, so it never appears on the rendered page.

questions.question:
A developer writes

expecting a self-closing element. What is the issue?
questions.hint: Think about which elements have no content and need no closing tag.
options: is a void element and should not have a closing tag
must always be lowercase or it breaks
Nothing is wrong; both tags are required
questions.explanation:
is a void (empty) element with no content, so it is written as
(or
in XHTML); a closing
tag is invalid.

questions.question: Which attribute should be added to the <html> tag to declare the page's primary language as English, helping screen readers and search engines? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It is a global attribute set to a language code like "en".
questions.explanation: Setting lang="en" on the <html> element tells assistive technology and browsers the document's language, improving accessibility and correct pronunciation.

questions.question: A page renders in browser "quirks mode" with odd box sizing. Which omission most likely caused this?
questions.hint: Quirks mode is triggered when one specific first line is missing.
questions.explanation: Without the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration at the top, browsers fall back to quirks mode, emulating old non-standard layout behaviour.

topics.title: Text & Formatting
topics.description: Mark up text with headings, paragraphs, line breaks, emphasis, quotations, code, and special characters using semantic, modern tags.

questions.question: Which element represents the most important top-level heading on a page?
questions.hint: Headings range from h1 (biggest) to h6 (smallest).
questions.explanation: <h1> is the highest-level heading and should describe the page's main topic; headings go down to <h6>.

questions.question: Which element defines a paragraph of text?
questions.hint: It is a single short letter.
questions.explanation:
The

element represents a paragraph; browsers add space above and below it by default.

questions.question: Which empty element inserts a single line break inside text? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: It is a void element often used inside addresses or poems.
questions.explanation: forces a line break without starting a new paragraph; it is a void element with no closing tag.

questions.question: Which element creates a horizontal thematic divider line between sections? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Two letters, a void element, often shown as a rule line.
questions.explanation: <hr> represents a thematic break (a shift of topic) and is rendered as a horizontal rule by default.

questions.question: Which pair of elements is the semantically correct way to mark emphasised and strongly important text?
questions.hint: Prefer the semantic tags over the purely presentational ones.
questions.explanation: <em> conveys stress emphasis and <strong> conveys strong importance; <i> and <b> are purely visual and carry no semantic meaning.

questions.question: Which element should wrap a multi-line block quotation from another source?
questions.hint: It is a block-level quote element, not the short inline one.
questions.explanation: <blockquote> marks a section quoted from another source; <q> is for short inline quotes and <cite> names a work's title.

questions.question: Which element displays a snippet of computer code in a monospaced inline style? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Four letters; it means exactly what it shows.
questions.explanation: The <code> element marks up a fragment of computer code and is typically rendered in a monospace font.

questions.question: Which character entity must you use to display a less-than sign as visible text instead of starting a tag?
questions.hint: It begins with an ampersand and ends with a semicolon.
questions.explanation: Because < starts a tag, you write the entity < to display a literal less-than sign; similarly > gives the greater-than sign and & gives the ampersand.

questions.question: Write markup for a section with a top-level heading "About Us" followed by a paragraph that reads "We make great tools."
questions.hint: Use an h1 then a p.
questions.explanation:
Headings (

) introduce content and paragraphs (

) hold the body text, giving the page a clear, accessible outline.

questions.question: Write a paragraph that says "Save your work often" where the word "often" is strongly important.
questions.hint: Wrap just the word often in <strong>.
questions.explanation: <strong> marks the word as having strong importance, and browsers render it bold while assistive tech may emphasise it.

questions.question: Write a preformatted block that preserves spacing and shows the two lines "line one" and an indented "line two" exactly as typed.
questions.hint: Use the <pre> element, which keeps whitespace and line breaks.
questions.explanation: The <pre> element preserves whitespace and newlines exactly as written, which is ideal for ASCII art or formatted code.

questions.question: Write a sentence with the chemical formula H2O where the 2 is shown as a subscript.
questions.hint: Use the <sub> element around the 2.
questions.explanation: <sub> renders text as subscript (lower and smaller); its counterpart <sup> renders superscript, useful for exponents and footnotes.

questions.question: A designer skips from <h1> straight to <h4> to make text smaller. Why is this a problem?
questions.hint: Heading levels describe document structure, not font size.
options: Heading levels are about visual size only, so it is fine
It breaks the document outline and harms accessibility; size should be set with CSS
<h4> cannot appear without an <h2> and <h3> being self-closed
Browsers will refuse to render the page
questions.explanation: Heading levels convey hierarchy for assistive technology and SEO; skipping levels for visual size confuses the outline — use CSS for sizing instead.

questions.question: You want to show that text was deleted and replacement text inserted, with semantic meaning. Which elements fit best?
questions.hint: There are dedicated edit-tracking elements in HTML.
questions.explanation: <del> marks removed content and <ins> marks inserted content, carrying edit semantics; <strike> is deprecated and <s> only means no-longer-accurate.

questions.question: Which element highlights text to mark it as relevant or as a search hit, typically shown with a yellow background? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: It means to highlight; four letters.
questions.explanation: The <mark> element represents text highlighted for reference or relevance, such as matched search terms, and is styled with a highlight by default.

topics.title: Links, Images & Lists
topics.description: Connect pages with anchors, embed images responsibly, and organise content with ordered, unordered, and description lists.

questions.question: Which element creates a hyperlink, and which attribute holds the destination URL?
questions.hint: The anchor element plus the hypertext reference attribute.
questions.explanation: The <a> (anchor) element creates a hyperlink, and its href attribute specifies the destination URL.

questions.question: Which attribute on provides alternative text for screen readers and broken images?
questions.hint: It describes the image when it cannot be seen.
questions.explanation: The alt attribute gives a text alternative for an image, read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load.

questions.question: Which attribute on points to the image file's location? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: Same attribute name used by scripts and media to give a source.
questions.explanation: The src (source) attribute holds the path or URL of the image to display.

questions.question: Which element creates an ordered (numbered) list? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Two letters: ordered list.
questions.explanation: <ol> creates an ordered list whose items (<li>) are automatically numbered; <ul> creates an unordered (bulleted) list.

questions.question: Which value of the target attribute opens a link in a new browser tab?
questions.hint: It refers to a blank browsing context.
questions.explanation: target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab or window; pair it with rel="noopener" for security.

questions.question: What does an href value of "#contact" do?
questions.hint: The hash refers to an element's id on the same page.
options: Jumps to the element with id="contact" on the page
questions.explanation: An href starting with # is a fragment link that scrolls to the element whose id matches, e.g. id="contact".

questions.question: Which element pairs with <ol> or <ul> to represent each individual list item? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Two letters: list item.
questions.explanation: Each entry in an ordered or unordered list is wrapped in an <li> (list item) element.

questions.question: In a description list, which element holds the term being described? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Description term — two letters.
questions.explanation: A description list <dl> pairs a description term <dt> with its description <dd>.

questions.question: Write a link with the text "Visit Example" that goes to https://example.com.
questions.hint: Use <a> with href and put the text between the tags.
questions.explanation: The anchor's href sets the destination and the text between the tags is the clickable label.

questions.question: Insert an image from "logo.png" with the alternative text "Company logo".
questions.hint: Use the void element with src and alt.
questions.explanation: is a void element; src gives the file and alt provides accessible alternative text.

questions.question: Write an unordered list of three fruits: Apple, Banana, Cherry.
questions.hint: Use <ul> with three <li> items.
questions.explanation: An unordered list <ul> displays each <li> with a bullet; the order of items is not meaningful.

questions.question: Write an ordered list giving the steps: Mix, Bake, Serve.
questions.hint: Use <ol> so the steps are numbered in sequence.
questions.explanation: <ol> numbers each <li> automatically, which is correct when sequence matters, as in recipe steps.

questions.question: Make an image at "hero.jpg" (alt "Mountain view") into a clickable link that opens https://photos.example.com in a new tab safely.
questions.hint: Wrap the in an using target="_blank" and rel="noopener".
questions.explanation: Placing an inside an makes the image a link; target="_blank" opens a new tab and rel="noopener" prevents the new page from accessing window.opener.

questions.question: An image is purely decorative and adds no information. What is the recommended alt value?
questions.hint: Screen readers should skip purely decorative images.
options: Leave out the alt attribute entirely
questions.explanation: An empty alt="" tells screen readers to ignore a decorative image; omitting alt entirely is invalid and may cause the filename to be read instead.

questions.question: Write a description list defining HTML as "Markup for structure" and CSS as "Styling for pages".
questions.hint: Use <dl> with <dt> for each term and <dd> for each definition.
questions.explanation: A description list <dl> groups term/description pairs, using <dt> for the term and <dd> for its description.

topics.title: Tables
topics.description: Build accessible data tables with rows, header and data cells, captions, column and row spans, and the thead, tbody and tfoot sections.

questions.question: Which element defines a table row?
questions.hint: Table row — abbreviated to two letters.
questions.explanation: <tr> defines a table row, inside which you place header cells (<th>) or data cells (<td>).

questions.question: Which element represents a header cell, typically bold and centered?
questions.hint: Table header cell.
questions.explanation: <th> marks a header cell that labels a column or row; browsers render it bold and centered by default.

questions.question: Which element holds a standard data cell inside a table row? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Table data — two letters.
questions.explanation: <td> defines a standard data cell within a <tr> row.

questions.question: Which element provides a title or caption for an entire table? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: It comes right after the opening <table> tag.
questions.explanation: <caption>, placed as the first child of <table>, gives the table an accessible title describing its contents.

questions.question: Which attribute makes a single cell stretch across multiple columns?
questions.hint: It spans columns.
questions.explanation: colspan="n" makes a cell occupy n columns; rowspan does the same vertically across rows.

questions.question: Which three sectioning elements group a table's header, body, and footer rows?
questions.hint: They all start with the letter t.
questions.explanation: <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> group the header, body, and footer rows, improving structure, accessibility, and printing.

questions.question: Which attribute would you set to "2" so a header cell stretches down over two rows? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It spans rows rather than columns.
questions.explanation: rowspan="2" makes a cell occupy two rows vertically, merging them in that column.

questions.question: On a <th>, which attribute set to "col" or "row" tells assistive tech which cells the header labels? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It defines the header's scope.
questions.explanation: The scope attribute (scope="col" or scope="row") associates a header cell with its column or row, greatly improving screen-reader navigation.

questions.question: Write a simple table with a header row "Name" and "Age", and one data row "Ann", "30".
questions.hint: Use <table>, a <tr> with <th> cells, and a <tr> with <td> cells.
questions.explanation: A table is built from rows (<tr>) containing header cells (<th>) and data cells (<td>).

questions.question: Write a table with a caption "Sales", a thead with headers "Q1" and "Q2", and a tbody row "100", "150".
questions.hint: Put <caption> first, then <thead> and <tbody> sections.
questions.explanation: A <caption> titles the table, <thead> groups the header row, and <tbody> groups the data rows for clear structure and accessibility.

questions.question: Write a table row where a single header cell "Totals" spans across two columns.
questions.hint: Use colspan="2" on the <th>.
questions.explanation: colspan="2" merges the cell so it covers two columns, which is useful for grouped headers.

questions.question: Add scope attributes to two column header cells "Item" and "Price" so screen readers associate them with their columns.
questions.hint: Each <th> should have scope="col".
questions.explanation: scope="col" ties each header to the cells beneath it in the same column, making the table navigable for assistive technology.

questions.question: A developer uses a table to lay out a page's columns of unrelated content. Why is this discouraged in modern HTML?
questions.hint: Tables carry meaning about tabular data.
options: Tables are slower to download than divs
Tables are only for tabular data; using them for layout harms semantics and accessibility — use CSS instead
Tables are not supported on mobile devices
questions.explanation: Tables semantically represent rows and columns of data; using them for visual layout confuses screen readers and breaks responsiveness. Layout should be done with CSS (flexbox/grid).

questions.question: In a table, make the first data cell "N/A" span two rows, then show its sibling cell "East" in the same row.
questions.hint: Apply rowspan="2" to the first <td> and add the sibling cell after it.
questions.explanation: rowspan="2" makes the first cell occupy this row and the next, so the following <tr> only needs one cell to fill the remaining column.

questions.question: Which table section element is intended for summary or total rows and may be rendered at the bottom even if written before the body? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Table footer.
questions.explanation: <tfoot> groups footer rows such as totals; browsers display it at the bottom of the table.

topics.title: Forms & Inputs
topics.description: Collect user data with forms: text and specialised inputs, labels, checkboxes, radios, selects, textareas, buttons, and built-in validation.

questions.question: Which element wraps a group of controls that are submitted together?
questions.hint: It is named after the concept it represents.
questions.explanation: The <form> element groups input controls and defines how and where their data is submitted via the action and method attributes.

questions.question: Which attribute associates a <label> with a specific input?
questions.hint: It refers to the input's id.
questions.explanation: A label's for attribute must match the input's id, linking them so clicking the label focuses the input and screen readers announce it.

questions.question: Which attribute on an <input> sends a value to the server under a given key? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It is the key part of the submitted key=value pair.
questions.explanation: The name attribute becomes the key in the submitted form data; inputs without a name are not submitted.

questions.question: Which input type masks the characters the user types? Answer with just the type value.
questions.hint: It is used for secret credentials.
questions.explanation: <input type="password"> hides typed characters (usually as dots) so passwords are not shown on screen.

questions.question: Which input type lets the user pick exactly one option from a mutually exclusive set sharing the same name?
questions.hint: Several of them, only one can be chosen.
questions.explanation: Radio buttons (type="radio") that share the same name form a group from which only one can be selected at a time.

questions.question: Which element creates a multi-line text box?
questions.hint: It is not an <input>; it is its own element.
questions.explanation: <textarea> is a dedicated element for multi-line text input; its size is set with the rows and cols attributes or CSS.

questions.question: Which boolean attribute on an input prevents the form from submitting until the field is filled in? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It marks the field as mandatory.
questions.explanation: The required boolean attribute triggers built-in validation, blocking submission until the field has a value.

questions.question: Which attribute shows faint sample text inside an empty input as a hint? Answer with just the attribute name.
questions.hint: It is a temporary hint that disappears when typing.
questions.explanation: The placeholder attribute shows hint text inside an empty field; it is not a substitute for a real <label>.

questions.question: Write a labelled text input for a username, linking the label and input correctly.
questions.hint: Use <label for> matching the input's id.
questions.explanation: Matching the label's for to the input's id creates an accessible association so clicking the label focuses the field.

questions.question: Write a form that posts to "/login" containing an email field and a submit button.
questions.hint: Set method="post" and action="/login"; use input type="email" and a submit button.
questions.code:
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
questions.explanation: The form's action and method define where and how data is sent; type="email" enables email validation and the submit button triggers submission.

questions.question: Write a dropdown select labelled "Country" with options United States and Canada.
questions.hint: Use <select> with <option> children, each with a value.
questions.code:
<label for="country">Country</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
  <option value="us">United States</option>
  <option value="ca">Canada</option>
</select>
questions.explanation: <select> creates a dropdown; each <option> has a value sent on submit and visible text shown to the user.

questions.question: Write a radio button group named "plan" offering "Free" and "Pro", each with a label.
questions.hint: Both inputs share name="plan" but have different ids and values.
questions.code:
<input type="radio" id="free" name="plan" value="free">
<label for="free">Free</label>
<input type="radio" id="pro" name="plan" value="pro">
<label for="pro">Pro</label>
questions.explanation: Sharing the same name groups the radios so only one can be selected; distinct ids let each pair with its own label.

questions.question: You need numeric input restricted to 1-10. Which combination best uses built-in validation?
questions.hint: Use a number input with min and max.
questions.explanation: type="number" with min="1" and max="10" provides numeric input plus automatic range validation and stepper controls.

questions.question: Group related shipping fields under a visible legend "Shipping address" using the proper grouping elements, containing one text input for street.
questions.hint: Use <fieldset> with a <legend> wrapping the labelled input.
questions.explanation: <fieldset> groups related controls and <legend> gives the group an accessible caption, helping users understand the form's structure.

questions.question: A placeholder is being used as the only label for an input. Why is this an accessibility problem?
questions.hint: Think about what happens once the user starts typing.
options: The placeholder disappears on input and is not reliably announced as a label by assistive tech, so use a real <label>
Placeholders are not supported in HTML5
questions.explanation: Placeholder text vanishes when the user types and is not a dependable accessible name; every control should have an associated <label>.

topics.title: Semantic HTML & Accessibility
topics.description: Use meaningful structural elements and accessibility features — landmarks, figures, ARIA, alt text and tab order — to build inclusive pages.

questions.question: Which element represents the main, unique content of a document, and should appear only once?
questions.hint: It is named after exactly that idea.
questions.explanation: <main> wraps the dominant content of the page and should be used only once per document, giving screen readers a key landmark.

questions.question: Which element best represents the site's primary navigation links?
questions.hint: Short word for navigation.
questions.explanation: <nav> marks a block of navigation links, a landmark that assistive technology can jump to directly.

questions.question: Which semantic element represents a self-contained, independently distributable piece of content like a blog post? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Think of a news or blog item.
questions.explanation: <article> represents a complete, self-contained composition (such as a blog post or news story) that could stand on its own.

questions.question: Which element represents tangentially related content such as a sidebar or pull quote? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: Five letters; content set to the side.
questions.explanation: <aside> marks content indirectly related to the main content, like a sidebar, callout, or set of related links.

questions.question: What is the key difference between <section> and <div>?
questions.hint: One carries meaning about a thematic grouping.
options: There is no difference; they are interchangeable
<section> is a thematic grouping with semantic meaning (usually with a heading), while <div> is a generic, meaningless container
questions.explanation: <section> denotes a thematic group of content, typically with a heading, whereas <div> is a generic container with no semantic meaning, used mainly for styling.

questions.question: Which pair of elements wraps an image with its associated caption?
questions.hint: One groups the media, the other captions it.
questions.explanation: <figure> groups self-contained media and <figcaption> provides its caption, associating the description with the content semantically.

questions.question: Which element typically holds introductory content or branding and navigation at the top of a page or section? Answer with just the tag name.
questions.hint: It sits at the top; do not confuse it with <head>.
questions.explanation: <header> contains introductory content such as a logo, site title, or section heading, and can appear at page or section level.

questions.question: Which ARIA attribute gives an interactive element an accessible name when no visible text label exists? Answer with the full attribute name.
questions.hint: It is an aria attribute that supplies a label string.
questions.explanation: aria-label provides an accessible name for an element (e.g. an icon-only button) that has no visible text for screen readers to announce.

questions.question: Write a semantic page skeleton with a header, a nav, a main, and a footer (each containing placeholder text).
questions.hint: Use the landmark elements directly inside the body.
questions.explanation: Using header, nav, main, and footer creates clear landmarks that let assistive technology and search engines understand the page structure.

questions.question: Write a figure containing an image "chart.png" (alt "Sales chart") with the caption "Quarterly sales".
questions.hint: Wrap the and a
questions.explanation: <figure> groups the image with its <figcaption>, semantically tying the caption to the visual it describes.

questions.question: Write an icon-only close button (containing a × character) that has an accessible name "Close".
questions.hint: Use aria-label to name the button for screen readers.
questions.explanation: Since the × glyph is not meaningful to screen readers, aria-label="Close" supplies a clear accessible name for the button.

questions.question: Write a self-contained blog post using the correct semantic element, with a heading "My Trip" and a paragraph "It was fun."
questions.hint:
Use
wrapping an

and a

.
questions.explanation: <article> marks the post as an independent, self-contained unit of content with its own heading and body.

questions.question: A page uses clickable <div> elements with onclick handlers as buttons. What accessibility problem does this cause?
questions.hint: Native buttons come with behaviour for free.
options: None; a div with onclick behaves exactly like a button
It is not keyboard focusable or operable and is not announced as a button, so a real <button> should be used
Divs cannot have click handlers at all
It makes the page load slower
questions.explanation: A plain <div> is not focusable, cannot be activated by keyboard, and is not exposed as a button to assistive tech; using a native <button> provides all of this automatically.

questions.question: Which tabindex value adds a normally non-interactive element to the natural tab order without disrupting normal tab flow?
questions.hint: Positive values reorder the tab sequence and are discouraged.
questions.explanation: tabindex="0" inserts the element into the natural tab order at its DOM position; positive values create confusing custom orders and tabindex="-1" makes an element focusable only via script.

questions.question: Which ARIA attribute set to "true" hides a purely decorative element from the accessibility tree? Give the full attribute name.
questions.hint: It hides content from assistive technology only.
questions.explanation: aria-hidden="true" removes an element (and its children) from the accessibility tree, useful for decorative icons that would otherwise add noise for screen-reader users.
